topic: After the Storm — De-resuscitation, Recovery & Post-Sepsis Syndrome
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Critical Care Complex
speakerBio: Returns to close the conference she helped open — from the failing organs of Session 13 to the de-resuscitation, recovery clinic, and survivorship that complete the sepsis journey.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Day 6. Your urosepsis patient from Session 13 has turned the corner — off vasopressors this morning, lactate cleared, source controlled. The team is delighted and moves on to the next crisis. But look at him: he is +11 litres cumulative fluid balance, oedematous to the thighs, still ventilated because his lungs are waterlogged, ICU-delirious, and profoundly weak. The sepsis is over; the consequences of surviving it are just beginning. This final session is about everything after the storm — getting the fluid back off, getting him off the ventilator and the ICU, and getting him a life worth the resuscitation. Then we close all sixteen sessions.

1 · 💧 De-resuscitation — the fourth phase nobody finishes

Resuscitation is only the first act. The ROSE model frames the whole fluid journey and reminds us the pendulum must swing back:

PhaseGoalFluid strategy
R — Resuscitation (mins–hours)Rescue perfusionRapid boluses, life-saving fluid
O — Optimisation (hours)Match supply to demandTitrated, fluid-responsiveness guided
S — Stabilisation (days)Organ support, avoid harmNeutral balance, minimal maintenance
E — Evacuation / De-escalation (days)Remove accumulated fluidNegative balance — active de-resuscitation
The fluid that saved the patient on day one is the fluid that drowns them on day four. Someone has to own the de-resuscitation.

Why it matters: a persistently positive cumulative fluid balance is independently associated with mortality, prolonged ventilation, and worse AKI. Once shock has resolved and the patient is stable off pressors, aim for neutral then negative balance — restrict maintenance fluids, stop "creep" (drug diluents, KVO lines), and use diuretics (or ultrafiltration/RRT if refractory) to offload. The FACTT trial in ARDS showed a conservative fluid strategy improved oxygenation and shortened ventilation without increasing shock or dialysis.

⚠️ De-resuscitate the stable, not the shocked

Negative balance is for the patient who is haemodynamically stable and off (or nearly off) vasopressors. Aggressively diuresing a patient who is still fluid-responsive and vasoplegic will crash the cardiac output and re-injure the kidney. The skill is timing: resuscitate hard early, then have the discipline to reverse it once the capillaries seal.

2 · 📉 Weaning vasopressors & liberating from support

As the vasoplegia resolves, wean noradrenaline down in steady steps while watching MAP and perfusion (lactate, urine output, mentation, capillary refill). Steroids started for shock (Session 13) are tapered as pressors come off. Liberate from the ventilator with daily spontaneous breathing trials paired with daily sedation interruption (the ABCDEF bundle: Assess pain, Both SATs/SBTs, Choice of light sedation, Delirium monitoring, Early mobility, Family engagement). Light sedation, minimal benzodiazepines, and early mobilisation are the levers that shorten ICU stay and reduce the syndrome we meet next.

3 · 🧩 Post-Intensive-Care Syndrome (PICS)

Surviving sepsis is not the same as recovering from it. PICS is the constellation of new or worsened impairments persisting after critical illness, across three domains:

DomainManifestationsDrivers
PhysicalICU-acquired weakness, critical-illness polyneuromyopathy, fatigue, breathlessness, reduced exercise toleranceImmobility, inflammation, catabolism, hyperglycaemia, steroids/NMBAs
CognitiveImpaired memory, attention, executive function — sometimes dementia-likeDelirium duration, hypoxia, sedation, neuroinflammation
PsychologicalAnxiety, depression, PTSD, sleep disturbanceDelirium, delusional ICU memories, mechanical ventilation

PICS-Family extends this to relatives — anxiety, depression, complicated grief, and PTSD in those who sat at the bedside. Delirium duration is the strongest modifiable risk factor for long-term cognitive impairment (BRAIN-ICU showed the more delirium days, the worse the cognition at 1 year), which is why the ABCDEF bundle is prevention, not just process.

4 · ⏳ Post-sepsis syndrome & the long tail of mortality

The danger does not end at ICU discharge. Sepsis survivors carry a persistently elevated mortality for months to years and a high burden of readmission:

  • Up to 1 in 3 sepsis survivors dies within the following year; a substantial fraction of in-hospital "sepsis deaths" actually occur after apparent recovery.
  • Roughly 40% are readmitted within 90 days — commonly with a recurrent or new infection, cardiovascular events, or AKI.
  • Survivors have elevated rates of new cardiovascular events, cognitive decline, and functional dependence.
Sepsis is a chronic disease with an acute presentation. Surviving to discharge is a milestone, not the finish line.
🎯 Post-sepsis syndrome

A recognised cluster of physical, cognitive, and psychological sequelae plus immune dysregulation that leaves survivors vulnerable to recurrent infection. It overlaps with PICS but specifically captures the persistent susceptibility to new sepsis — the immune system does not simply reset to normal.

5 · 🔥 Chronic critical illness & PICS-CCI

Some patients neither die nor recover — they enter chronic critical illness: prolonged dependence on organ support (often the ventilator via tracheostomy), recurrent infections, and a downward spiral driven by PICS-CCI — Persistent Inflammation, Immunosuppression, and Catabolism Syndrome.

💡 The PICS-CCI engine

Persistent inflammation (ongoing low-grade cytokine drive, raised CRP, expansion of myeloid-derived suppressor cells) + immunosuppression (lymphopenia, T-cell exhaustion → recurrent nosocomial and reactivated infections) + catabolism (relentless muscle wasting, hypoalbuminaemia, poor wound healing, sarcopenia). Each feeds the others in a self-sustaining vicious cycle — the chronic mirror image of the acute cytokine storm.

Management is not a single drug but a bundle: aggressive nutrition and protein delivery, early and sustained rehabilitation, infection surveillance and prevention, minimising further immunosuppressive insults, and realistic, honest goals-of-care conversations. Many of these patients will not return to their premorbid state, and prognostic honesty is part of good care.

6 · 🏃 Rehabilitation & structured follow-up

  • Early rehabilitation — physiotherapy and mobilisation begun in the ICU, continued through the ward and into the community, is the core treatment for ICU-acquired weakness.
  • Nutrition — adequate protein to counter catabolism; dietitian involvement; screen and treat refeeding risk.
  • Post-ICU / post-sepsis follow-up clinics — structured review of the three PICS domains, medication reconciliation, and screening for anxiety/depression/PTSD and cognitive impairment.
  • An ICU diary and psychological support reduce PTSD by filling the delusional memory gaps of the illness.
  • Medication reconciliation — deliberately stop drugs that were only for the acute phase (e.g. PPIs started for stress-ulcer prophylaxis, antipsychotics started for ICU delirium) so they are not continued for life by inertia.

7 · 🛡️ Secondary prevention — closing the infection loop

Because survivors are readmitted with recurrent infection, prevention is active treatment:

  • Vaccination — pneumococcal and annual influenza (and COVID-19) for survivors; the full asplenia bundle if relevant (Session 14).
  • Eradicate the source — remove the stone, close the perforation, definitively fix the biliary obstruction, exchange or remove long-term lines and catheters; ensure the source-control job started acutely is actually finished.
  • Optimise comorbidities — glycaemic control, nutrition, and functional status all reduce reinfection risk.
  • Safety-net education — teach the survivor and family to recognise early sepsis and seek help fast, since their threshold to re-septic is low.

8 · 📊 Stewardship & quality improvement — closing the system loop

The final loop is at the level of the hospital, not the patient. Antimicrobial stewardship and QI metrics are how a unit keeps getting better:

LeverWhat good looks like
De-escalationNarrow the spectrum to culture results at 48–72 h; stop redundant cover
DurationShortest effective course (e.g. ~4 days post source control, STOP-IT; procalcitonin can support stopping)
IV-to-oral switchConvert early once stable and absorbing
Bundle complianceAudit the SSC hour-1 bundle: cultures, lactate, antibiotics, fluids, pressors
Outcome metricsTime-to-antibiotics, bundle compliance, mortality, readmission, C. difficile & resistance rates

Stewardship is not the enemy of sepsis care — it is its maturation. Give broad and fast at hour one; then narrow, shorten, switch, and stop. That is how you protect both this patient and the next one from resistance.

☠️ M&M — the survivor everyone forgot to follow up

A 67-year-old woman survived pneumococcal septic shock after a two-week ICU stay and went home "cured," +9 L in balance at ward transfer, on an antipsychotic started for ICU delirium and a PPI started for stress-ulcer prophylaxis — both continued on the discharge summary with no stop date. Nobody vaccinated her. Nobody arranged rehab. Over the next three months she was profoundly weak (ICU-acquired weakness never addressed), became depressed and frightened (undiagnosed PICS), fell twice on the antipsychotic, and was readmitted at week 10 with a second pneumococcal pneumonia — the vaccine she never got. She died on that admission. Lessons: discharge is the most dangerous handover in sepsis. De-resuscitate the fluid, reconcile and stop the acute-only drugs, screen and treat the three PICS domains, arrange rehabilitation, and vaccinate and eradicate the source — the resuscitation is not complete until the survivor has a plan to stay alive.

9 · 🏁 The whole conference — sixteen sessions in one breath

We opened this conference at the bedside of a crashing patient and we close it at the bedside of a survivor. The arc:

  1. Sepsis is a dysregulated host response, not just an infection — Sepsis-3, SOFA, and the endothelium.
  2. Recognise it early — NEWS2/qSOFA screening; the deteriorating patient hides in plain sight.
  3. The hour-1 bundle saves lives — cultures, lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics fast, fluids, and pressors for MAP ≥65.
  4. Resuscitate to dynamic targets — lactate clearance and fluid-responsiveness, not a fixed CVP.
  5. Noradrenaline first, then vasopressin, then steroids for the shock that won't lift.
  6. Antimicrobials: right drug, right dose, fast — then de-escalate.
  7. Find the source and control it — the drain, the knife, the removed line (S15).
  8. Read the organ failures through the SOFA — AKI, ARDS, cardiomyopathy, DIC, liver, brain, adrenal (S13).
  9. The broken-defence host hides the fire — neutropenic, asplenic, transplant sepsis (S14).
  10. Match syndrome to bug to drug to source control (S15).
  11. Then de-resuscitate — swing the fluid pendulum back (S16).
  12. Liberate — wean pressors and ventilator with the ABCDEF bundle.
  13. Beware PICS — physical, cognitive, psychological — delirium is the modifiable driver.
  14. Sepsis is a chronic disease — a long tail of mortality, readmission, and PICS-CCI.
  15. Rehabilitate, follow up, and prevent the next one — vaccinate, eradicate the source, reconcile the drugs.
  16. Steward the antibiotics and audit the system — narrow, shorten, switch, stop; measure, and improve.
Give broad and fast at hour one; find and control the source; support the failing organs; then have the discipline to de-resuscitate, liberate, and follow up. Sepsis care is a loop — and the loop only closes when the survivor stays alive.

You have travelled from the first dysregulated cytokine to the post-sepsis clinic. Thank you for attending all sixteen sessions.

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Finish the fluid job — the ROSE model ends in Evacuation; a persistently positive balance kills, so de-resuscitate the stabilised patient toward neutral/negative (FACTT).
  2. Liberate deliberately — wean pressors and ventilate off with the ABCDEF bundle; light sedation and early mobility shorten stay.
  3. PICS is the price of survival — physical, cognitive, psychological (and family); delirium duration is the strongest modifiable driver.
  4. Sepsis is chronic — up to a third die within a year and ~40% are readmitted; post-sepsis syndrome leaves immune vulnerability.
  5. PICS-CCI = persistent inflammation + immunosuppression + catabolism — a self-sustaining vicious cycle needing nutrition, rehab, and honesty.
  6. Prevent the next one — vaccinate, eradicate the source, reconcile and stop acute-only drugs, and safety-net the survivor.
  7. Close the system loop — stewardship (de-escalate, shorten, switch, stop) and QI metrics protect this patient and the next.

moderatorQs.q: What is de-resuscitation and when in the ROSE model does it belong?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: De-resuscitation is the active removal of accumulated fluid once shock has resolved — the E (Evacuation/De-escalation) phase of the ROSE model, following Resuscitation, Optimisation and Stabilisation. It matters because a persistently positive cumulative fluid balance is independently associated with mortality, prolonged ventilation and worse AKI, and FACTT showed a conservative fluid strategy improves oxygenation and shortens ventilation. The critical safeguard is timing: only de-resuscitate the patient who is haemodynamically stable and off (or nearly off) vasopressors — restrict maintenance, stop fluid creep, and diurese (or ultrafiltrate) toward neutral then negative balance. Aggressively offloading a still-vasoplegic, fluid-responsive patient will crash cardiac output and re-injure the kidney.

moderatorQs.q: Define PICS and name its strongest modifiable risk factor.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Post-Intensive-Care Syndrome (PICS) is new or worsened impairment after critical illness across three domains — physical (ICU-acquired weakness, critical-illness polyneuromyopathy, fatigue), cognitive (memory, attention and executive dysfunction, sometimes dementia-like), and psychological (anxiety, depression, PTSD) — with PICS-Family affecting relatives. The strongest modifiable risk factor for long-term cognitive impairment is duration of delirium — BRAIN-ICU showed more delirium days predict worse cognition at one year. That is precisely why the ABCDEF bundle (light sedation, daily awakening and breathing trials, delirium monitoring, early mobility, minimal benzodiazepines) is genuine prevention, not just process.

moderatorQs.q: In what sense is sepsis a chronic disease, and what does that mean for discharge?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because surviving to discharge is a milestone, not a cure. Sepsis survivors carry a persistently elevated mortality — up to a third die within the following year — and around 40% are readmitted within 90 days, frequently with recurrent or new infection, cardiovascular events, or AKI, on a background of post-sepsis immune dysregulation. So discharge must be an active intervention, not a full stop: de-resuscitate the fluid, reconcile and stop acute-only drugs (stress-ulcer PPIs, ICU antipsychotics), screen and treat the three PICS domains, arrange rehabilitation and follow-up, and deliver secondary prevention — vaccination, source eradication, and safety-net education. The resuscitation is not complete until the survivor has a plan to stay alive.

audienceQs.q: My patient is off pressors and +12 L. How aggressively should I diurese?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Now is exactly the right time to de-resuscitate. Once the patient is haemodynamically stable and off (or nearly off) vasopressors, aim for neutral then negative fluid balance: cut maintenance fluids, eliminate fluid creep (drug diluents, keep-vein-open lines, unnecessary flushes), and use loop diuretics — an infusion if boluses are inadequate — titrated to perfusion, not just urine output. If diuresis fails and there is refractory overload, ultrafiltration/RRT is the tool. Watch lactate, MAP and mentation as you offload; if the patient becomes hypotensive or oliguric from falling preload, you have gone too fast. FACTT supports this conservative-once-stable approach — better oxygenation and shorter ventilation without more shock or dialysis.

audienceQs.q: What actually reduces ICU-acquired weakness and PICS?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Early mobilisation and rehabilitation started in the ICU is the core treatment — passive then active exercises begun while still ventilated, continued through the ward and into the community. It works best embedded in the ABCDEF bundle: pairing daily sedation interruption with spontaneous breathing trials and keeping sedation light (minimising benzodiazepines) means the patient is awake enough to move and less delirious, which in turn protects long-term cognition. Add adequate protein/nutrition to counter catabolism, delirium-prevention measures (orientation, sleep, family engagement), and structured post-ICU follow-up. The combination shortens ventilation and ICU stay and reduces the physical and cognitive burden of PICS.

audienceQs.q: Which medications should we deliberately stop before a sepsis survivor goes home?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Do a proper medication reconciliation and stop the drugs that were only ever for the acute phase — the classic culprits continued by inertia are PPIs started for stress-ulcer prophylaxis and antipsychotics started for ICU delirium (which cause falls and sedation if carried on indefinitely). Review and de-escalate antibiotics to the shortest effective course (around 4 days after adequate source control, per STOP-IT; procalcitonin can support stopping) and complete the IV-to-oral switch. At the same time, make sure the preventive medications are actively added — pneumococcal and influenza vaccination, and the full asplenia bundle if relevant — because these survivors are readmitted with recurrent infection.
